cim_eredeti: Right to control likeness recommended by Australia's AI inquiry
szoveg_eredeti:
Labor and Coalition join bipartisan call for compensation of creatives while incentivizing AI to train onshore

CANBERRA — Australians could gain a Denmark-style right to control how their face, voice and likeness are used under recommendations to government from the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence.

The committee, due to report to parliament on Tuesday, makes that recommendation among 45 others, including weighing in on the controversy about how best to balance the rights of copyright holders with the desire of the Australian government to train artificial intelligence models onshore.

In October Denmark proposed an amendment to copyright law, still before its parliament, to give individuals legal rights over their appearance, body, and voice against unauthorized AI deepfakes and digital replicas. The proposal is also being pushed in the EU by left-wing parties.

The Australian joint select committee, chaired by Labor MP Jo Briskey with retiring Liberal senator Jonno Duniam as deputy chair, has attempted to find common ground on how to attract AI investment.

Australia is a middle power in the middle of tension. Sitting on a quarter of the world's uranium and lithium, part way through a divisive energy transition, and at the start of its bigger defense investment — nuclear submarines — Australia is at the leading edge of many of the world's toughest power and policy debates. If you're tracking AUKUS, critical minerals, tech regulation, energy trade-offs, or the rise of nationalism, Canberra is no longer optional reading.
